00 Overview
One app, built twice. Read this first, then step through the files in order.

Cortex is a chatbot with two jobs: an agent that remembers past conversations and can search the web, and a RAG pipeline that answers questions from uploaded PDFs. cortex-core builds everything by hand on the raw OpenAI, transformers and chromadb libraries. cortex-langgraph rebuilds the same app on LangChain components and LangGraph graphs, keeping prompts, defaults and behavior the same so the two can be compared fairly.

The pattern to look for
Almost every change is one of two moves. LangChain replaces a hand-written interface (model, embeddings, vector store, prompt, splitter) with a standard one that every provider implements. LangGraph replaces hand-written control flow (the tool loop, the RAG steps, the fallback policy) with a graph of nodes and edges you can see, bound and trace.

01 model.py
src/business/core/model.py · 183 → 147 lines · 258 rows changed

How the app talks to a chat model. cortex-core wrote its own model interface; LangChain already ships one that every provider implements.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • A hand-written BaseLLM abstract class with one method, generate(question, context).
  • Two implementations: OpenAIModel wraps the raw OpenAI client, LocalHFModel drives transformers + torch directly (tokenizer, model.generate, decode, strip the prompt).
  • build_azure_openai_client() returns a raw client so the agent can do tool calling separately.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • No interface of its own: create_llm() returns a LangChain BaseChatModel (ChatOpenAI, AzureChatOpenAI or ChatHuggingFace).
  • Every provider is called the same way: llm.invoke(messages) returns an AIMessage.
  • Built-in retries (max_retries=5) and tool calling (.bind_tools()) on the same object.
  • model_label() reads the model name back for metrics, whichever provider it is.

Why it matters: Every response now carries token usage (AIMessage.usage_metadata). cortex-core never reported tokens, so its cost tracking could never run.

BaseChatModelChatOpenAIAzureChatOpenAIChatHuggingFace

1#Here is the openai LLM model implementation1"""Chat model factory — LangChain edition.
2
3In cortex-core this file held a hand-written `BaseLLM` interface with two
4implementations (`OpenAIModel` wrapping the raw OpenAI client, `LocalHFModel`
5wrapping transformers + torch directly), each with its own `generate()`.
6
7LangChain already defines that interface: `BaseChatModel`. Every provider
8package ships an implementation of it, so the three branches below just pick
9one. Everything downstream (the RAG graph, the agent graph) only ever sees a
10`BaseChatModel` and calls `.invoke()` / `.bind_tools()` on it — it never
11knows which provider is behind it.
12
13What LangChain gives us for free compared to cortex-core:
14- One call shape for every provider: `llm.invoke(messages) -> AIMessage`.
15- Token usage on every response (`AIMessage.usage_metadata`), which cortex-core
16 never surfaced — that is what finally makes cost tracking work end-to-end.
17- Tool calling (`.bind_tools()`) on the same object, so the agent no longer
18 needs a separate raw OpenAI client.
19- Built-in retries (`max_retries`).
20"""
21

13# Base LLM Interface
14class BaseLLM(ABC):
15 @abstractmethod
16 def generate(self, question: str, context: list[str]) -> str:
17 pass
18# abstractmethod used when you have 2 or more models that you will decide to use which one to use at runtime
19
20#HuggingFace Local LLM Implementation
21class LocalHFModel(BaseLLM):
22 """
23 Wrapper for openai LLMs to generate responses based on prompts.
24 Local Hugging Face Model Implementation
25 suitable for on-prem or offline inference
26 """
27 def __init__(self, model_name: str, system_prompt: str, max_input_tokens: int = 2048, max_output_tokens: int = 512):
28
29 self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
30 self.model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name)
31 self.prompt_builder = PromptBuilder(system_prompt)
32 self.max_input_tokens = max_input_tokens
33 self.max_output_tokens = max_output_tokens
34
35 if self.tokenizer.pad_token is None:
36 self.tokenizer.pad_token = self.tokenizer.eos_token
37 """
38 Simple meaning:
39 If the tokenizer does not define a padding token,
40 the end-of-sequence (EOS) token is used as the padding token.
41
42 Explanation:
43 The pad_token is required to make all sequences in a batch the same length.
44
45 Example:
46 "Hello"
47 "Hello how are you"
48
49 Converted to tensors:
50 [Hello, <PAD>, <PAD>]
51 [Hello, how, are, you]
52
53 Without a pad_token, batch processing will fail and raise runtime errors.
54
55 The eos_token (End Of Sequence) indicates the end of a sentence.
56 Many autoregressive models (e.g., GPT-style):
57 - Are not designed for batch padding
58 - Do not define a pad_token (pad_token = None)
59 - Only provide an eos_token
60
61 Using EOS as PAD:
62 - Prevents crashes and runtime errors
63 - Does not negatively affect attention mechanisms
64 - Is a common and safe practice during inference
65 """
66 def generate(self, question: str, context: list[str]) -> str:
67 """
68 Generates a response from the LLM based on the provided question and context.
69
70 Args:
71 question (str): The user's question or input.
72 context (list): Relevant context passages retrieved from the knowledge base.
73 max_length (int): Maximum length of the generated response.
74
75 Returns:
76 str: The generated response from the LLM.
77 """
78 prompt = self.prompt_builder.build_prompt(question, context)
79 inputs = self.tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True,max_length=self.max_input_tokens)
80
81 with torch.no_grad():
82 outputs = self.model.generate(**inputs, max_length=self.max_input_tokens, pad_token_id=self.tokenizer.eos_token_id)
83
84 generated_text = self.tokenizer.decode(outputs[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
85 # Extract only the part after the prompt
86 return generated_text[len(prompt):].strip()
87

90class OpenAIModel(BaseLLM):
91 def __init__(self, client: OpenAI, model_name: str, system_prompt:str, temperature: float = 0.7, max_tokens: int = 512):
92 self.client = client
93 self.model_name = model_name
94 self.temperature = temperature
95 self.max_tokens = max_tokens
96 self.prompt_builder = PromptBuilder(system_prompt)
97 def generate(self, question: str, context: list[str]) -> str:
98 """
99 Generates a response from the OpenAI LLM based on the provided question and context.
100 Args:
101 question (str): The user's question or input.
102 context (list): Relevant context passages retrieved from the knowledge base.
103 Returns:
104 str: The generated response from the LLM.
105 """
106 messages = self.prompt_builder.build_messages(question, context)
107 response = self.client.chat.completions.create(
108 model=self.model_name,
109 messages=messages,
110 max_tokens=self.max_tokens,
111 temperature=self.temperature
112 )
113 return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

02 embedding.py
src/business/core/embedding.py · 112 → 120 lines · 143 rows changed

Turning text into vectors. Same two methods on both sides; LangChain removes the hand-written retry loop and adds a cache.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • A hand-written Embedder abstract class with embed_documents() and embed_query().
  • OpenAIEmbedder calls client.embeddings.create() and retries 500 errors with its own exponential-backoff loop.
  • Azure works by injecting an AzureOpenAI client into the same class.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • Returns LangChain's Embeddings interface: OpenAIEmbeddings or AzureOpenAIEmbeddings, retries built in.
  • Optional on-disk cache (CacheBackedEmbeddings + LocalFileStore), keyed by a SHA-256 hash of the text and namespaced by provider and model.
  • Vector stores take the embedder directly, so the stores embed text themselves.

Why it matters: Re-indexing the same PDF re-embeds identical chunks. With the cache those come from disk instead of a paid API call.

EmbeddingsOpenAIEmbeddingsCacheBackedEmbeddings

1"""Embedding interfaces and OpenAI implementation."""1"""Embedding factory — LangChain edition.
2
3cortex-core defined its own `Embedder` ABC and an `OpenAIEmbedder` with a
4hand-rolled exponential-backoff retry loop. LangChain's `Embeddings` interface
5has the same two methods (`embed_documents`, `embed_query`), and
6`OpenAIEmbeddings` / `AzureOpenAIEmbeddings` implement it with retries built in.
7
8Because every LangChain vector store takes an `Embeddings` object directly,
9the vector stores now embed text themselves — callers hand them strings /
10Documents instead of pre-computed vectors.
11
12New compared to cortex-core: an optional on-disk embedding cache
13(`CacheBackedEmbeddings`). Re-indexing the same PDF re-embeds identical chunks;
14with the cache those come from disk instead of a paid API call.
15"""

14class Embedder(ABC):
15 @abstractmethod
16 def embed_documents(self, texts: List[str]) -> List[List[float]]:
17 ...
18
19 @abstractmethod
20 def embed_query(self, text: str) -> List[float]:
21 ...
22
23 def embed(self, text: str) -> List[float]:
24 """
25 Alias for embed_query() for backward compatibility with LongTermMemory.
26 """
27 return self.embed_query(text)

30class OpenAIEmbedder(Embedder):
31 """
32 Thin wrapper over OpenAI embeddings.
33 Uses text-embedding-3-small by default (fast, 1536 dims).
34 """
35
36 def __init__(
37 self,
38 api_key: Optional[str] = None,
39 model: str = "text-embedding-3-small",
40 client: Optional[OpenAI] = None,
41 ):
42 # `client` lets callers (e.g. the Azure branch of create_embedder())
43 # inject a pre-built AzureOpenAI client — it's duck-type compatible
44 # since only .embeddings.create() is ever called on it.
45 self.client = client or OpenAI(api_key=api_key)
46 self.model = model
47
48 def _embed(self, inputs: List[str], max_retries: int = 5) -> List[List[float]]:
49 last_err = None
50 for attempt in range(max_retries):
51 try:
52 res = self.client.embeddings.create(model=self.model, input=inputs)
53 return [item.embedding for item in res.data]
54 except InternalServerError as e:
55 last_err = e
56 if attempt < max_retries - 1:
57 delay = 2 ** attempt
58 time.sleep(delay)
59 print(f"⚠️ OpenAI 500 error, retrying in {delay}s (attempt {attempt + 2}/{max_retries})...", flush=True)
60 else:
61 raise last_err from None
62 raise last_err from None
63
64 def embed_documents(self, texts: List[str]) -> List[List[float]]:
65 if not texts:
66 return []
67 return self._embed(texts)
68
69 def embed_query(self, text: str) -> List[float]:
70 return self._embed([text])[0]

94def with_embedding_cache(embedder: Embeddings, *, cache_dir: str, namespace: str) -> Embeddings:
95 """Wrap an embedder so repeated texts are served from a local file cache.
96
97 The namespace includes provider + model: vectors from different models are
98 not interchangeable, so they must never share cache entries.
99 query_embedding_cache=True caches query embeddings too (same store), so a
100 repeated question skips the embedding call as well.
101 """
102 from langchain_classic.embeddings import CacheBackedEmbeddings
103 from langchain_classic.storage import LocalFileStore
104
105 # The namespace becomes part of every cache key, and LocalFileStore only
106 # accepts [A-Za-z0-9_.-/] in keys — "openai:text-embedding-3-small" would
107 # be rejected on the first write. Replace anything else (and "/", which
108 # would create subdirectories) with "_".
109 safe_namespace = re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9_.\-]", "_", namespace)
110
111 store = LocalFileStore(cache_dir)
112 return CacheBackedEmbeddings.from_bytes_store(
113 embedder,
114 store,
115 namespace=safe_namespace,
116 query_embedding_cache=True,
117 # Keys are a hash of the text. The default (SHA-1) isn't
118 # collision-resistant and LangChain warns about it; SHA-256 is.
119 key_encoder="sha256",
112 )120 )

03 agentic_chatbot.py
src/business/chatbot/agentic_chatbot.py · 306 → 285 lines · 273 rows changed

The agent loop: call the model, run any tools it asks for, repeat until it answers. Same loop, but LangGraph turns it into a graph.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • A while True: loop in _agent_loop(): call chat.completions.create(tools=...), run each tool call, append the results, repeat.
  • No cap on the number of rounds, so a model that keeps asking for tools loops forever.
  • Tools are a hand-written JSON schema list (TOOLS) plus an if tool_name == ... dispatcher.
  • Returns the answer text only; token usage is never collected.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • A StateGraph with two nodes: agent (the model with tools bound) and tools (LangGraph's prebuilt ToolNode).
  • tools_condition routes to tools or END; recursion_limit caps it at 10 tool rounds.
  • MessagesState appends each step's messages, so nodes only return what's new.
  • Sums usage_metadata across every model call in the turn into last_usage.

Why it matters: The loop is identical in behavior, but the graph is bounded, can be drawn, streamed step by step and traced. Memory (Redis, Chroma, SQLite) is unchanged.

3# VectorDB -> for free-form queries (e.g., knowledge retrieval, document search)
4# This chatbot should use the SQL database of each user like last location, last search, etc.
5# to make the conversation more personalized and context-aware. For example, when user ask about the trip suggestion
6# it can use the last location of the user to suggest nearby attractions or restaurants.

10Memory architecture:4Memory architecture (unchanged from cortex-core):
11 Short-term → RedisMemory (recent turns, auto-expires)5 Short-term → RedisMemory (recent turns, auto-expires)
12 Long-term → LongTermMemory / VectorDB (semantic search over all history)6 Long-term → LongTermMemory (semantic search over all history, Chroma)
7 Persistent → ChatHistoryManager (SQLite, survives restarts; feeds the history API)

18After every chat() turn the exchange is persisted to the vector store so11cortex-core ran a hand-written `while True:` loop — call the model, if it asked
19future turns can recall it semantically.12for tools run them and append the results, repeat until it answers in plain
13text. Here that loop is a LangGraph `StateGraph` with two nodes:
14
15 ┌─────────┐ tools_condition: model asked for tools? ┌─────────┐
16 START │ agent │ ───────────────────── yes ────────────────▶ │ tools │
17 ────▶ │ (LLM) │ ◀────────────────────────────────────────── │ToolNode │
18 └────┬────┘ └─────────┘
19 │ no (plain answer)
20 ▼
21 END
22
23- `agent` calls the chat model with the tools bound (`llm.bind_tools`).
24- `tools` is LangGraph's prebuilt `ToolNode`: it runs every tool call in the
25 last AI message and appends one ToolMessage per call.
26- `tools_condition` is the prebuilt router that picks between the two.
27
28The loop is the same; what the graph adds is that it's inspectable (you can
29draw it, stream each step, trace it) and bounded — LangGraph stops a runaway
30loop at `recursion_limit` (see MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS) instead of spinning forever.
31
32Why short-term memory is NOT a LangGraph checkpointer: the official Redis
33checkpointer needs Redis with the JSON and Search modules (Redis Stack / Redis 8
34with the query engine). Plain Redis — what Docker Compose, Homebrew and Azure
35Cache for Redis Basic/Standard provide — doesn't have them. So conversation
36turns stay in plain Redis lists, and are converted to LangChain messages when
37they enter the graph.

62# Upper bound on agent → tools round-trips per user turn. cortex-core's
63# while-loop had no cap at all, and LangGraph's own default (10,007 steps) is
64# effectively none either. Each round is two graph steps (agent, then tools);
65# the final answer needs two more (the answering agent step, and the step that
66# reaches END). Exceeding it raises GraphRecursionError.
67# It means LangGraph puts a safety limit on how many times the agent can call tools in one user request.
68#If you configure max_tool_rounds = 5, the agent can make at most 5 tool-call rounds.
69#If it exceeds the limit, LangGraph raises GraphRecursionError.
70
71MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 10
72RECURSION_LIMIT = 2 * MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS + 2

200 def _agent_loop(self, messages: List[Dict]) -> str:
201 """
202 Runs the ReAct loop: call LLM → handle tool calls → repeat until the
203 model returns a plain text response.

205 while True:
206 response = self.client.chat.completions.create(

218 result = self._handle_tool_call(

220 json.loads(tc.function.arguments),
221 )
222 messages.append({
223 "role": "tool",
224 "tool_call_id": tc.id,
225 "content": result,
226 })
227 else:
228 return msg.content

255 #These are two helper functions that process the messages produced by the LangGraph run.
256 # extract the final answer from the model.
257 @staticmethod
258 def _final_text(new_messages: List[BaseMessage]) -> str:
259 """The graph ends on the model's plain-text answer — the last AIMessage."""
260 for message in reversed(new_messages):
261 if isinstance(message, AIMessage):
262 # .text flattens both plain-string and content-block responses.
263 return message.text
264 return ""
265
266 @staticmethod
267 #Purpose: calculate the total token usage for the entire user turn.
268 def _sum_usage(new_messages: List[BaseMessage]) -> Dict[str, int]:
269 """Add up token usage across every model call made during this turn.
270
271 A turn with two tool rounds calls the model three times; cortex-core
272 never reported tokens at all, so cost tracking could never fire.
273 """
274 totals = {"input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": 0, "total_tokens": 0}
275 for message in new_messages:
276 usage = getattr(message, "usage_metadata", None)
277 if usage:
278 for key in totals:
279 totals[key] += int(usage.get(key, 0) or 0)
280 return totals
281
282
283# So these functions are not LangGraph orchestration.
284# They are application-level helpers used after/during
285# the graph execution to extract the result and track usage/cost.

04 tools.py
src/business/chatbot/tools.py · 85 → 75 lines · 82 rows changed

The agent's two tools, search_vector_db and web_search. New file in cortex-langgraph; the left side is the cortex-core code it replaces.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • Each tool existed twice: once as a JSON schema in AgenticChatbot.TOOLS, once as a branch in _handle_tool_call().
  • Keeping schema, name and arguments in sync between the two was manual.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • Each tool is a plain function with @tool. LangChain builds the JSON schema from the signature and docstring.
  • LangGraph's ToolNode does the dispatch, so there's no if/elif chain.
  • build_tools() gives the tools their user, memory store and search provider by closure.

Why it matters: The function is the tool, so the schema can't drift from the code. Tool names and descriptions are unchanged, so the model sees exactly the same tools.

05 chatbot/__init__.py
src/business/chatbot/__init__.py · 129 → 124 lines · 30 rows changed

Wiring: builds the chatbot and its memory for each request. Small diff, but it's where the real token counts reach the API.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • Builds the vector store, then passes the embedder and an _IdentityChunker to LongTermMemory.
  • The API response hardcodes model_used: "gpt-4o" and tokens_used: None.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • The embedder goes into the vector store instead, and LongTermMemory(vectorstore=...) needs nothing else.
  • Returns the real model name plus tokens_used, input_tokens and output_tokens from chatbot.last_usage.

Why it matters: With real token counts, the controller's cost-tracking branch finally runs.

06 prompt_builder.py
src/business/core/prompt_builder.py · 141 → 152 lines · 156 rows changed

How prompts are assembled. Wording is identical on purpose so the two apps can be compared fairly; only the mechanism changes.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • A PromptBuilder class builds prompts with f-strings: build_prompt_text(), build_messages() (OpenAI message dicts) and build_prompt().
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • The same wording lives in LangChain templates: build_rag_prompt() returns a ChatPromptTemplate, and the agent prompt is a PromptTemplate.
  • format_context() formats LangChain Documents for the prompt.
  • A template is a Runnable, so the RAG graph can pipe it straight into the model: prompt | llm.

Why it matters: Templates compose with | and show up as their own step in LangSmith / Langfuse traces.

src/business/rag/retrieval.py · 78 → 182 lines · 159 rows changed

The RAG pipeline: retrieve, re-rank, then answer. cortex-core ran it as three calls in a row; cortex-langgraph makes each step a graph node.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • RAGPipeline.answer() embeds the question, queries the store, re-ranks, then calls the model.
  • _retrieve() parses Chroma's raw nested-list response into RetrievedChunk objects.
  • What happens when the re-ranker rejects everything is buried inside select_context() in orchestrator.py.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • A StateGraph: retrieve → rerank → generate, with fallback and refuse branches.
  • The fallback policy (fail_closed / fail_open / hybrid) is a visible conditional edge, _route_after_rerank().
  • generate is an LCEL chain: ChatPromptTemplate | chat model | StrOutputParser.
  • State records confidence (high / low / none) to show which branch ran.

Why it matters: The safety decision ("refuse or fall back when nothing relevant was found") is now part of the graph you can see, instead of hidden in a helper function.

1"""Retrieve → rerank → prompt → generate."""1"""RAG pipeline — a LangGraph StateGraph.
2
3cortex-core's `RAGPipeline.answer()` was three function calls in a row, with
4the "what if the re-ranker rejects everything?" policy buried inside
5`select_context()`. Here each step is a node and that policy is a visible
6branch:
7
8 START → retrieve → rerank ──(chunks passed the gate)──────────────▶ generate → END
9 │ ▲
10 ├──(nothing passed, policy fail_open/hybrid)──▶ fallback
11 │
12 └──(nothing passed, policy fail_closed)───────▶ refuse → END
13
14- retrieve VectorStore.similarity_search_with_score — dense top-k (default 30)
15- rerank cross-encoder score → relevance gate → sort → top-n (default 8)
16- fallback gate rejected everything: use the raw vector top-n, confidence "low"
17- refuse fail_closed policy: don't call the LLM at all
18- generate ChatPromptTemplate | chat model | StrOutputParser (an LCEL chain)
19
20Every node reads the shared state and returns only the keys it changes; LangGraph
21merges them. `confidence` records which branch ran — "high" (re-ranked),
22"low" (fallback) or "none" (refused) — and query_rag() turns it into metrics.

153 # ------------------------------------------------------------------ graph
154 def _build_graph(self):
155 builder = StateGraph(RAGState)
156 builder.add_node("retrieve", self._retrieve)
157 builder.add_node("rerank", self._rerank)
158 builder.add_node("fallback", self._fallback)
159 builder.add_node("refuse", self._refuse)
160 builder.add_node("generate", self._generate)
161
162 builder.add_edge(START, "retrieve")
163 builder.add_edge("retrieve", "rerank")
164 builder.add_conditional_edges(
165 "rerank",
166 self._route_after_rerank,
167 {"generate": "generate", "fallback": "fallback", "refuse": "refuse"},
168 )
169 builder.add_edge("fallback", "generate")
170 builder.add_edge("generate", END)
171 builder.add_edge("refuse", END)
172 return builder.compile()
173
174 # -------------------------------------------------------------------- API
175 def run(self, question: str) -> RAGState:
176 """Run the graph and return its final state."""
177 return self.graph.invoke({"question": question})
178

180 """Answer a question. Returns (answer, context chunks, confidence)."""
181 state = self.run(question)
182 return state["answer"], state.get("context", []), state.get("confidence", "none")

08 vector_store.py
src/business/rag/vector_store.py · 261 → 147 lines · 316 rows changed

Where PDF chunks are stored and searched. The biggest reduction in code: LangChain's VectorStore interface replaces two hand-written backends.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • A hand-written VectorStoreBase (reset / upsert / query) with two backends: ChromaVectorStore and AzureSearchVectorStore.
  • The Azure backend translates Azure Search results into Chroma's nested-list shape, because retrieval.py parsed exactly that shape.
  • Callers embed text first and pass in raw vectors.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • create_vector_store() returns a LangChain VectorStore: langchain_chroma.Chroma or AzureSearch.
  • Both return (Document, score) pairs from similarity_search_with_score(), so no translation layer is needed.
  • The store owns its embedding model and embeds text itself.
  • Uses a different Azure index name, because LangChain's index schema isn't compatible with cortex-core's.

Why it matters: Swapping backends no longer means writing a new adapter class and a response translator.

VectorStoreChromaAzureSearchDocument

165 def upsert(
166 self,
167 ids: List[str],
168 embeddings: List[List[float]],
169 metadatas: List[Dict[str, Any]],
170 documents: List[str],
171 ) -> None:
172 if len(ids) != len(embeddings):
173 raise ValueError("ids and embeddings length mismatch")
174
175 docs = []
176 for doc_id, embedding, metadata, text in zip(ids, embeddings, metadatas, documents):
177 metadata = metadata or {}
178 docs.append({
179 "id": doc_id,
180 "content": text,
181 "embedding": embedding,
182 "source_id": str(metadata.get("source_id", "")),
183 "section": str(metadata.get("section", "")),
184 "chunk_start": int(metadata.get("chunk_start", 0)),
185 "chunk_end": int(metadata.get("chunk_end", 0)),
186 "chunk_strategy": str(metadata.get("chunk_strategy", "")),
187 })
188 self._search_client.merge_or_upload_documents(documents=docs)

190 def query(self, query_embedding: List[float], top_k: int = 15):
191 from azure.search.documents.models import VectorizedQuery
192
193 vector_query = VectorizedQuery(vector=query_embedding, k_nearest_neighbors=top_k, fields="embedding")
194 results = self._search_client.search(search_text=None, vector_queries=[vector_query], top=top_k)
195
196 ids: List[str] = []
197 docs: List[str] = []
198 metas: List[Dict[str, Any]] = []
199 scores: List[float] = []
200 for r in results:
201 ids.append(r["id"])
202 docs.append(r.get("content", ""))
203 metas.append({key: r.get(key) for key in self.INDEX_FIELDS_METADATA_KEYS})
204 # Azure Search's vector-query score is a similarity score (higher =
205 # better); Chroma's "distances" are a distance (lower = better).
206 # Negate it so "lower is better" holds for both backends — nothing
207 # downstream treats this as a calibrated distance, it's only ever
208 # used for display and (already-sorted) ordering.
209 scores.append(-float(r.get("@search.score", 0.0)))
210
211 # Match ChromaVectorStore.query()'s response shape exactly (outer list
212 # = batch of queries; we only ever send one) since retrieval.py's
213 # _retrieve() depends on this exact structure regardless of backend.
214 return {
215 "ids": [ids],
216 "documents": [docs],
217 "metadatas": [metas],
218 "distances": [scores],
219 }

Building the search index from PDFs: load, split, store. Each step is now a LangChain component.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • ingest_directory() → a custom Chunker per document → embed each batch → store.upsert() with raw vectors.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • DoclingLoader → RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter → VectorStore.add_documents().
  • add_documents() embeds and upserts in one call.

Why it matters: The pipeline shrinks to three calls, and every stage speaks the same Document type.

src/business/rag/pdfingest/pdf_digest.py · 150 → 122 lines · 159 rows changed

Reading PDFs. Docling does the parsing on both sides (locally, no API key); only the wrapper changes.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • Walks Docling's document model by hand: text blocks, then tables appended after a TABLES FROM DOCUMENT IMAGES separator.
  • Returns a custom IngestedDocument dataclass.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • langchain_docling.DoclingLoader turns each PDF into LangChain Documents.
  • Tables are exported as Markdown inline, where they appear, next to the text that explains them.
  • Noise (page headers, footers, captions) is dropped by Docling's own labels= filter; a MetaExtractor adds document metadata.

Why it matters: Keeping a table next to its explaining text gives the retriever better chunks.

Splitting documents into chunks. Same size and overlap; smarter cut points.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • A fixed character window: every chunk is exactly chunk_size characters, cut wherever the window ends, often mid-word.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with the same defaults (800 characters, 100 overlap) tries paragraph breaks first, then lines, sentences and words.
  • Keeps cortex-core's stable chunk ids (a hash of source, offset and text), so re-indexing overwrites instead of duplicating.

Why it matters: Chunks that end on natural boundaries read better to both the embedding model and the LLM.

src/memory/vectordb.py · 131 → 66 lines · 127 rows changed

The vector store behind conversation memory, kept separate from the PDF index on purpose.

cortex-core · hand-written
  • A hand-written ChromaVectorDB adapter (add / search / delete) over chromadb.Client.
  • In chromadb 1.x, Client(Settings(persist_directory=...)) is in-memory, so long-term memory was lost on every restart.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • langchain_chroma.Chroma(persist_directory=...) implements the VectorStore interface and really persists to disk.
  • Its own provider switch (CHAT_VECTOR_STORE_PROVIDER), separate from the RAG store's.

Why it matters: Besides removing the adapter, the migration fixed a real bug: memories now survive restarts.

ChromaVectorStore

1"""Conversation-memory vector store — LangChain edition.

3This is the chatbot's long-term-memory index — a separate index from the RAG
4vector store (src/business/rag/vector_store.py). Kept separate by design: RAG
5chunks (PDF content) and per-user conversation history serve different
6purposes and shouldn't share an index.
7
8cortex-core wrapped chromadb by hand in a `ChromaVectorDB` adapter with its own
9`add/search/delete` interface. LangChain's `VectorStore` is that interface, and
10`langchain_chroma.Chroma` implements it — including embedding the text itself,

13Behavior note: cortex-core created `chromadb.Client(Settings(persist_directory=...))`,

15and long-term memory was lost on every restart. Chroma(persist_directory=...)
16here really persists, so memories now survive restarts.

A command-line check of raw retrieval (no re-ranking, no LLM).

cortex-core · hand-written
  • Builds the whole RAGPipeline and calls its private _retrieve() method.
cortex-langgraph · LangChain / LangGraph
  • Calls store.similarity_search_with_score() directly: the standard, public LangChain API.

Why it matters: No reaching into a class's private methods to test one step.
